Summary

In 1290, England mourned the death of a queen, Eleanor of Castile, beloved wife of King Edward I. Her body was carried on a 200-mile journey from Lincoln to London, a solemn procession that would become immortalized in stone. To mark the places where her cortege rested, a heartbroken Edward commissioned twelve magnificent Eleanor Crosses. More than seven centuries later, historian Alice Loxton set herself an epic challenge: following in history's footsteps by walking the entire 200-mile funeral route on the corresponding dates. As Alice journeys in search of England's forgotten queen, over ancient paths and modern motorways, history comes alive in surprising ways.

Cementing a reputation

Following the route of the Eleanor crosses
Mary Hitchman
Book Details

Alice Loxton

Eleanor
A 200-mile walk in search of England’s lost queen 352pp. Pan Macmillan. £22.
Many are commemorated in stone, but few so grandly as Eleanor of Castile ( d . 1290). Following her unexpected death in Lincolnshire, her husband, Edward I, commissioned twelve ornate monuments to mark the journey her body took to London. Three of these Eleanor crosses still stand today. In this book, Alice Loxton traces the route of the nineteen-day funeral procession to see the monuments or their sites, and learn about Eleanor along the way.
Loxton undertook her journey on foot in winter, at the same time of year as Eleanor’s procession, and invites the reader to think about the queen’s layered history as she walks.

(family, friends, servants). After Eleanor’s death, Edward wrote of her: “who in life we dearly cherished and who in death we cannot cease to love”. Their love story, and Edward’s grief, is a recurring theme.
The book is particularly good at drawing together the different versions of Eleanor’s commemoration.

...

Rather than “a memorial prompted by Edward’s broken heart”, the Eleanor crosses likely had an additional function as propaganda. The building project was a highly visible attempt at reputation rehabilitation which, over 700 years later, found its mark.

The story of the Eleanor Crosses: Finding Eleanor with Alice Loxton

By retracing the funeral route of the Eleanor Crosses on foot, historian Alice Loxton discovered the transformative power of walking through England’s history at a human pace.
Author:
Alice Loxton
Updated Date:

Add us as a preferred source on Google

On 28 November 1290, Eleanor of Castile – one of the most formidable medieval queens, and wife of Edward I – died suddenly in the village of Harby, in Nottinghamshire. Her body was taken to nearby Lincoln, where it was embalmed. Then, in December 1290, in an epic procession almost 200 miles long, her coffin was taken on the road south to London, and honoured with “great devotion, with services and holy vigils”. Her funeral took place in Westminster Abbey on 17 December, and she was buried in a magnificent tomb beside the shrine of Edward the Confessor.
The 36-year marriage of Edward and Eleanor was a rarity of the medieval world: a royal marriage of true, devoted love.
